grammarRules.title: Definite Articles
grammarRules.explanation: German has three definite articles: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter). The choice depends on the gender and case of the noun. Memorizing the gender of each noun is essential for correct German grammar.
grammarRules.germanExplanation: Das Deutsche hat drei bestimmte Artikel: der (männlich), die (weiblich), das (sächlich). Die Wahl hängt vom Genus und Kasus des Substantivs ab. Das Einprägen des Genus jedes Substantivs ist für die korrekte deutsche Grammatik unerlässlich.

exercises.question: Which article is used for 'Mann' (man)?
exercises.explanation: Mann is a masculine noun, so it uses the definite article 'der'.

exercises.question: Complete: '___ Frau kommt aus der Schweiz.' (The woman comes from Switzerland.)
exercises.explanation: Frau is a feminine noun, so it uses the definite article 'die'.

exercises.question: Translate 'the book' to German:
exercises.explanation: Buch is a neuter noun, so it uses the definite article 'das'.

grammarRules.title: Indefinite Articles
grammarRules.explanation: German indefinite articles correspond to 'a/an' in English. They are: ein (masculine), eine (feminine), ein (neuter). Note that masculine and neuter use the same form 'ein'.

exercises.question: Which indefinite article is used for 'Frau' (woman)?
exercises.explanation: Frau is a feminine noun, so it uses the indefinite article 'eine'.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Ich habe ___ Buch.' (I have a book.)
exercises.explanation: Buch is a neuter noun, so it uses the indefinite article 'ein'.

grammarRules.title: Present Tense - Regular Verbs
grammarRules.explanation: Regular German verbs follow a predictable pattern in the present tense. Remove the -en ending and add the appropriate personal ending for each pronoun.

exercises.question: Conjugate 'spielen' (to play) for 'du':
exercises.explanation: Remove -en from spielen to get spiel-, then add -st for du.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Wir ___ Deutsch.' (We speak German.)
exercises.explanation: For wir, use the infinitive form with -en ending.

exercises.question: Create a sentence using 'arbeiten' (to work) in present tense:
exercises.explanation: A basic German sentence follows Subject-Verb-Object order.

grammarRules.title: Present Tense - Irregular Verbs
grammarRules.explanation: Some common German verbs are irregular in the present tense. They often have vowel changes in the 2nd and 3rd person singular (du and er/sie/es).

exercises.question: Conjugate 'lesen' (to read) for 'er':
exercises.explanation: Lesen has a vowel change from e to ie in the 3rd person singular.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Ich ___ ein Buch.' (I read a book.)
exercises.explanation: For ich, lesen becomes lese without vowel change.

grammarRules.title: Noun Plurals
grammarRules.explanation: German nouns have several plural formation patterns. There are no universal rules, but common patterns include adding -e, -er, -en, or -s, sometimes with umlaut changes.

exercises.question: What is the plural of 'der Stuhl' (chair)?
exercises.explanation: Stuhl follows the -e pattern with umlaut change.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Das Auto → ___ Autos' (The car → the cars)
exercises.explanation: All plural nouns in German use the definite article 'die'.

grammarRules.title: Possessive Articles
grammarRules.explanation: Possessive articles indicate ownership or relationship. They change based on the gender of the possessed noun and the person who possesses it.

exercises.question: Which possessive article is correct: '___ Hund' (my dog)?
exercises.explanation: Hund is masculine, so it uses 'mein' in the nominative case.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Das ist ___ Katze.' (This is your cat.)
exercises.explanation: Katze is feminine, so it uses 'deine' for informal 'your'.

grammarRules.title: Accusative Case
grammarRules.explanation: The accusative case is used for direct objects (the receiver of the action). Only masculine articles change in the accusative case.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Ich habe ___ Apfel.' (I have the apple.)
exercises.hint: Apfel is masculine and it's a direct object
exercises.explanation: Apfel is masculine and is the direct object, so it uses 'den' in the accusative case.

exercises.question: Create a sentence with 'kaufen' (to buy) and 'Stuhl' (chair):
exercises.explanation: Stuhl is masculine and is the direct object, so it uses 'den'.

grammarRules.title: Separable Verbs
grammarRules.explanation: Separable verbs have prefixes that detach from the main verb and move to the end of the sentence in the present tense. Common prefixes include an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, nach-, vor-, zu-.

exercises.question: Create a sentence with 'anrufen' (to call):
exercises.explanation: In anrufen, the prefix an- separates and goes to the end.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Wir ___ heute ein.' (We shop today.)
exercises.explanation: The main verb kaufen stays in position 2, ein- goes to the end.

grammarRules.title: Modal Verbs
grammarRules.explanation: Modal verbs express ability, permission, obligation, or desire. The main modal verbs are: können (can), wollen (want), müssen (must), dürfen (may), sollen (should), mögen (like). They are conjugated irregularly and are followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause.

examples.english: He wants to go to Berlin.

exercises.question: Conjugate 'können' for 'du':
exercises.explanation: Können has an irregular conjugation: du kannst.

exercises.question: Create a sentence with 'wollen' and 'spielen':
exercises.explanation: Modal verbs are followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause.

grammarRules.title: Perfect Tense (Perfekt)
grammarRules.explanation: The perfect tense is used for completed actions in the past. It's formed with an auxiliary verb (haben or sein) in the present tense plus the past participle. Most verbs use haben, but verbs of motion, state change, or certain special verbs use sein.

exercises.question: Which auxiliary verb is correct: 'Ich ___ gegessen.'?
exercises.explanation: Essen is a regular verb that uses haben as the auxiliary.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Er ___ nach Berlin gefahren.' (He has gone to Berlin.)
exercises.hint: fahren is a verb of motion
exercises.explanation: Fahren is a verb of motion, so it uses sein as the auxiliary.

grammarRules.title: Dative Case
grammarRules.explanation: The dative case is used for indirect objects (the recipient of something). It's also used with certain prepositions and verbs. All articles change in the dative case.

examples.german: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.
examples.english: I give the man the book.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Ich helfe ___ Frau.' (I help the woman.)
exercises.hint: Frau is feminine and it's an indirect object
exercises.explanation: Frau is feminine and is the indirect object, so it uses 'der' in the dative case.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Wir sprechen ___ Lehrer.' (We speak with the teacher.)
exercises.explanation: Mit is a dative preposition, and Lehrer is masculine, so it becomes 'mit dem'.

grammarRules.title: Genitive Case
grammarRules.explanation: The genitive case shows possession or relationship. It's less commonly used in spoken German but important for formal writing and understanding written texts.

examples.german: Das ist das Auto des Mannes.
Die Tasche der Frau ist neu.
Das Spielzeug des Kindes ist bunt.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Das Haus ___ Nachbarn ist groß.' (The neighbor's house is big.)
exercises.explanation: Nachbar is masculine and shows possession, so it uses 'des' in the genitive case.

exercises.question: Create a sentence showing possession with 'Buch' and 'Student':
exercises.correct: Das ist das Buch des Studenten.
exercises.explanation: Student is masculine, so it becomes 'des Studenten' in the genitive case.

grammarRules.title: Adjective Declension
grammarRules.explanation: Adjectives in German change their endings based on the gender, case, and article of the noun they describe. There are three types of declension: strong, weak, and mixed.

exercises.question: Complete: 'der ___ Mann' (the good man)
exercises.explanation: With the definite article 'der', the adjective takes the weak ending '-e'.

exercises.question: Complete: '___ Wein' (good wine - no article)
exercises.explanation: Without an article, the adjective takes the strong ending '-er' for masculine nominative.

grammarRules.title: Comparative and Superlative
grammarRules.explanation: German adjectives form comparatives and superlatives to compare things. Comparative adds -er, superlative adds -st(e). Some adjectives have irregular forms.

exercises.question: What is the comparative of 'alt' (old)?
exercises.explanation: Alt has a vowel change from a to ä in the comparative, adding -er.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Das ist ___ Haus.' (This is the highest house.)
exercises.explanation: Hoch becomes höchste in the superlative with definite article.

grammarRules.title: Subordinate Clauses
grammarRules.explanation: Subordinate clauses add complexity to German sentences. They are introduced by conjunctions like weil (because), dass (that), wenn (when), ob (whether). The verb moves to the end of subordinate clauses.

examples.german: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland leben möchte.
examples.english: I am learning German because I want to live in Germany.
examples.translation: أتعلم الألمانية لأنني أريد العيش في ألمانيا.

examples.german: Er sagt, dass er müde ist.
examples.english: He says that he is tired.

examples.german: Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.
examples.english: When it rains, I stay at home.

tables.title: Common Subordinate Conjunctions
rows: Ich komme, weil ich Zeit habe.
Ich denke, dass es richtig ist.
Wenn du kommst, bin ich da.
Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt.
Obwohl es kalt ist, gehe ich raus.

exercises.question: Choose the correct conjunction: 'Ich bleibe zu Hause, ___ ich müde bin.'
exercises.explanation: Weil introduces a reason clause, so it's the correct choice here.

exercises.question: Create a sentence with 'dass' (that):
exercises.hint: Verb goes to end of subordinate clause
exercises.explanation: In subordinate clauses with dass, the conjugated verb moves to the end.

grammarRules.title: Relative Clauses
grammarRules.explanation: Relative clauses provide additional information about nouns. They are introduced by relative pronouns (der, die, das, die, deren, dessen) which change based on gender, case, and function in the clause. The verb moves to the end of relative clauses.

examples.german: Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Lehrer.
examples.english: The man who is standing there is my teacher.
examples.translation: الرجل الذي يقف هناك هو معلمي.

examples.german: Das Buch, das ich lese, ist interessant.
examples.english: The book that I am reading is interesting.

examples.german: Die Frau, deren Auto blau ist, kommt aus Berlin.
examples.english: The woman whose car is blue comes from Berlin.
examples.translation: المرأة التي سيارتها زرقاء قادمة من برلين.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Das Kind, ___ spielt, ist meine Tochter.' (The child who plays is my daughter.)
exercises.hint: Kind is neuter and subject of the clause
exercises.explanation: Kind is neuter and is the subject in the relative clause, so it uses 'das'.

exercises.question: Create a sentence with a relative clause about 'Frau' and 'arbeitet':
exercises.correct: Die Frau, die dort arbeitet, ist meine Chefin.
exercises.explanation: Frau is feminine, so it uses 'die' as the relative pronoun, and the verb goes to the end.

grammarRules.title: Passive Voice
grammarRules.explanation: The passive voice emphasizes the action rather than the agent. It's formed with werden + past participle (present passive) or wurde + past participle (past passive). The agent can be mentioned with 'von' or 'durch'.

examples.german: Die Tür wird von mir geöffnet.
examples.english: The door is opened by me.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Der Brief ___ geschrieben.' (The letter is written.)
exercises.explanation: For present passive, use wird + past participle.

exercises.question: Create a passive sentence with 'machen' (to do):
exercises.explanation: Passive voice uses werden + past participle (gemacht).

grammarRules.title: Subjunctive I (Konjunktiv I)
grammarRules.explanation: Subjunctive I is used for indirect speech, reporting what someone else said without confirming it. It's formed from the infinitive stem + subjunctive endings. It's mainly used in formal writing and news reporting.

examples.english: She thinks she will come tomorrow.

examples.german: Der Bericht besagt, das Unternehmen wachse.
examples.english: The report states that the company is growing.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Er sagt, er ___ krank.' (He says he is sick.)
exercises.explanation: For indirect speech, use the subjunctive I form 'sei' instead of 'ist'.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Sie meint, sie ___ das Buch.' (She thinks she has the book.)
exercises.explanation: For indirect speech, use the subjunctive I form 'habe' instead of 'hat'.

grammarRules.title: Subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II)
grammarRules.explanation: Subjunctive II is used for unreal situations, wishes, polite requests, and conditional sentences. It's formed from the simple past stem + subjunctive endings, often with umlaut changes. For irregular verbs, würde + infinitive is commonly used.

examples.german: Wenn ich Geld hätte, würde ich ein Haus kaufen.
examples.english: If I had money, I would buy a house.
examples.translation: لو كان لدي مال، لاشتريت منزلاً.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Wenn ich du ___, würde ich lernen.' (If I were you, I would study.)
exercises.explanation: For unreal conditional sentences, use the subjunctive II form 'wäre'.

exercises.question: Create a wish sentence with 'wünschte' and 'könnte':
exercises.explanation: Wishes use subjunctive II: ich wünschte + subjunctive II clause.

grammarRules.title: Conditional Sentences
grammarRules.explanation: Conditional sentences express conditions and their consequences. German uses wenn (if) for the condition clause and subjunctive II for unreal conditions. There are real conditions (indicative) and unreal conditions (subjunctive II).

examples.german: Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.
examples.english: If it rains, I stay at home.

examples.german: Wenn ich Geld hätte, würde ich reisen.
examples.english: If I had money, I would travel.

examples.german: Hätte ich mehr Zeit, würde ich Deutsch lernen.
examples.english: If I had more time, I would learn German.
examples.translation: لو كان لدي وقت أكثر، لتعلمت الألمانية.

tables.title: Conditional Sentence Types
rows: Wenn es kalt ist, trage ich einen Mantel.
Wenn ich Geld hätte, würde ich ein Auto kaufen.
Wenn ich gewusst hätte, wäre ich gekommen.

exercises.question: Complete: '___ ich Zeit hätte, würde ich dich besuchen.' (___ I had time, I would visit you.)
exercises.explanation: Wenn introduces conditional clauses, both real and unreal.

exercises.question: Create an unreal conditional sentence about having a car:
exercises.correct: Wenn ich ein Auto hätte, würde ich zur Arbeit fahren.
exercises.explanation: Unreal conditions use subjunctive II in the condition and würde + infinitive in the main clause.

grammarRules.title: Prepositions and Cases
grammarRules.explanation: German prepositions govern specific cases. Some always take one case (accusative, dative, or genitive), while two-way prepositions can take either accusative or dative depending on context (motion vs. location).

examples.german: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.english: The book is on the table.

examples.german: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
examples.english: I put the book on the table.

tables.title: Two-Way Prepositions
rows: neben den Stuhl (next to the chair)
neben dem Stuhl (next to the chair)
vor das Haus (in front of the house)
vor dem Haus (in front of the house)

exercises.question: Complete: 'Ich gehe ___ Kino.' (I go to the cinema.)
exercises.explanation: With motion to a place, use accusative case: in + das becomes ins.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Das Bild hängt ___ Wand.' (The picture hangs on the wall.)
exercises.explanation: With location (no motion), use dative case: an + der becomes an der.
